extracted.intended_audience: PR practitioners, in-house communicators, marketers and agency staff who write press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for choosing and applying tone of voice in press releases to increase credibility and journalist pickup. Covers high-level approach (journalistic vs achievement) and concrete stylistic rules (third person, active voice, plain language, measurable claims, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Tone of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone of voice refers to how your press release sounds and feels to readers — not just what you say but how you say it; it encompasses word choices, sentence structure, level of formality, and the overall impression your writing creates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone shapes perception and directly influences whether journalists take your announcement seriously. Two releases can announce identical news but be received very differently depending on tone. Use tone to convey credibility and avoid sounding sales-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer journalistic tone over achievement tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Two main approaches: journalistic (neutral, descriptive, fact-focused) and achievement (upbeat, celebratory, full of superlatives). The journalistic tone reads like a news article; the achievement tone sounds like marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic tone consistently outperforms achievement tone for media coverage — when your release sounds like news, journalists treat it like news; when it sounds like marketing, they ignore it. Reserve achievement tone for company blogs or promotional channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep it professional but human
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to sound credible and authoritative while still being readable — not robotic or overly formal, and not too casual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly formal constructions that nobody uses in conversation, but don't be too casual. Read the release aloud; if it sounds like a credible news broadcast, it's likely appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in third person
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to your organization by name rather than using 'we,' 'us,' or 'our' to create distance and objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'TechCorp announced today...' vs 'We’re thrilled to announce...'. Use first person only in direct quotes from spokespersons, which naturally represent spoken language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer constructions that put the actor before the action to create direct, engaging sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare: 'The company launched a new sustainability initiative' (active) vs 'A new sustainability initiative was launched by the company' (passive). Active voice produces shorter, clearer sentences that journalists can quote and adapt more easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon and buzzwords
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not stuff releases with overused terms that have lost specific meaning (e.g., 'synergy,' 'cutting-edge,' 'leverage,' 'best-in-class').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in plain language anyone can understand. Replace vague corporate speak ('leveraging innovative solutions to optimize operational efficiency') with concrete descriptions ('using new software to reduce processing time'). Buzzword-filled text signals lack of substance to journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay factual, not promotional
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release is intended to inform, not to sell; avoid presenting opinions as facts or using unverifiable superlatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrases like 'the best product on the market' or 'truly revolutionary technology.' Instead, describe what the product does and provide verifiable details and metrics where possible so readers can draw their own conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use measurable, verifiable claims instead of unsupported superlatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer concrete, quantifiable statements (e.g., 'reduces processing time by half') over vague claims ('dramatically improves efficiency').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurable statements are more credible and easier for journalists to verify and incorporate. Where possible, include numbers, test results, timelines, or specific outcomes rather than adjectives of praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tone to the announcement type
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the release’s energy and seriousness to suit the subject (e.g., product launch vs quarterly earnings vs crisis response).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product launch may carry slightly more energy than an earnings report; a crisis response requires a sober tone. Maintain overall brand voice consistency even when making these adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sentences must establish credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists form an opinion within the first few sentences; the lead should signal newsworthiness and competence immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a clear, factual lead that states the core news and context so a journalist can quickly assess relevance. Avoid burying key facts or surrounding them with hype that undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make content quote-ready and easy for journalists to use
rubrics_metrics.description: Write statements and quotes that a reporter can lift or adapt directly without heavy editing to remove marketing language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use active voice, third person, and factual claims. Keep direct quotes natural and appropriate; use first person only inside quotes. Avoid promotional language journalists will have to strip out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain, clear language
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate the same idea in straightforward terms so any reader (and any journalist) can understand it quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace complex corporate phrasing with simple descriptions of what the product/service does and who it helps. Plain language increases usability and reduces the chance journalists discard the release as incomprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive enthusiasm and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on exclamation points or breathless phrasing to convey importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive enthusiasm reads like advertising. Limit exclamation points and tone that suggests hype; let facts and concrete details demonstrate significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent brand voice across releases
rubrics_metrics.description: All press releases should feel like they come from the same organization even when covering different topics or adjusting tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create and follow internal standards for formality, attribution, and style so that adjustments for subject matter don't produce jarring inconsistencies that confuse journalists or audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unverifiable promotional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present opinions as facts; promotional claims should be supported or omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you assert superiority ('industry-leading,' 'game-changing'), back it with evidence or specific differentiators; otherwise, describe differences concretely and let readers draw conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limitations of a single-format press release and plan multi-channel distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A standalone press release depends on journalists deciding to cover your story and reaches only one audience/format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider adapting your announcement for other channels (news articles, blogs, videos, podcasts, social posts) and match tone/style to each format to reach audiences who don't rely on news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone appropriately by target format/platform
rubrics_metrics.description: When transforming the core announcement into other formats, calibrate tone and style to the platform: formal for news articles, conversational for podcasts, concise/attention-grabbing for social posts, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the core message remains consistent while the tone and style change to suit audience expectations on each channel. Use specialists or tools to optimize each format rather than republishing the same copy everywhere.
